synopsis: Decision-side nuisance braking occurs when sensors detect a real object but the logic incorrectly treats it as a collision; relevant operating situations include loading near piles, berm contact, spotters, and tight-clearance maneuvers [f13973, f13974, f13975]. The booklet identifies nuisance interventions as the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems and the main reason operators disable them, but suppressing all interventions in loading zones or repeated berm alarms would also conceal genuine hazards [f13982, f13980, f13981]. Context-aware approaches include Volvo’s remembered-slope logic and University of Pretoria’s 2024 steering-trajectory research, although the latter’s initial results are simulation-only [f1384, f6331]. Validation should include dedicated benign-but-dangerous-looking scenarios, drawing on road false-activation tests; millions of benign interactions may occur per imminent collision, making absence of hazardous braking harder to establish than a few successful stops [f1992, f15415, f1994, f1993]. Tuning should minimize nuisance subject to hard safety constraints rather than pursue zero false brakes: evidence for the optimum off-road trade-off is thin, no off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found, and the program must derive its acceptance threshold from shadow-mode data before enabling braking [f7312, f7460, f6570, f13984, f13985, f14058].
